name: The Dakota
facts: Designed by Henry J. Hardenbergh, who later designed the Plaza Hotel.
A popular legend says it was named because the Upper West Side felt as remote as the Dakota Territory. Historians doubt the story.
John Lennon lived here, and the exterior stood in for the Bramford in Rosemary's Baby (1968).

news.text: On September 23, 2026, construction workers used a crane to reach and repair one of The Dakota’s turrets, while crews cordoned off part of the West 72nd Street and Central Park West corner.

name: Flatiron Building
facts: Designed by Daniel Burnham's firm and first named the Fuller Building.
New Yorkers nicknamed it the Flatiron for its triangular shape, and the name stuck.
The gusts that whip around its narrow prow are part of the folklore behind the phrase "23 skidoo."

news.text: In August, The Guardian reported that the Flatiron Building was due to open as a residential building later that fall, with a double-height lobby, pool and a games room featuring a billiards table.

name: Hotel Chelsea
facts: Opened in the 1880s as one of the city's early cooperative apartment houses, then became a hotel.
Arthur C. Clarke worked on 2001: A Space Odyssey while living here.
Leonard Cohen wrote "Chelsea Hotel #2" about it.
Longtime manager Stanley Bard was known for accepting art from struggling artists in place of rent.
In Room 829, Thomas Wolfe produced the manuscript for You Can’t Go Home Again.
His editor published the novel posthumously in 1940.

In May 1938, Wolfe drew inspiration by roaming the hallways; sweltering New York heat made him say he could smell seven million inhabitants, and he used a Purdue speaking invitation as an excuse to leave.

name: Empire State Building
facts: Built in just over a year and opened in May 1931.
The top was designed as a mooring mast for airships. It never worked in practice.
It has its own ZIP code: 10118.

news.text: On Sept. 8, the Empire State Building Observation Deck opened a free field-trip request program for NYC public and charter schools, with visits for groups of up to 50 guests.
In July, the building announced its 48th annual Run-Up for Oct. 6: 225 runners would climb 1,576 stairs to the 86th-floor Observation Deck.

After a sold-out first event, the building announced four themed silent-disco nights on the 86th-floor deck from Sept. 19 to Oct. 17, with wireless LED headphones, a live DJ, and nighttime skyline views.

name: Chrysler Building
facts: Architect William Van Alen had the spire assembled secretly inside the tower, then hoisted it into place to claim the title of world's tallest building.
The steel eagles and radiator-cap ornaments nod to Chrysler cars.

news.text: On September 22, police closed streets near the Chrysler Building after an NYPD canine detected something inside an unattended suitcase; they evacuated a nearby building and cleared the package about 90 minutes later.

name: Woolworth Building
facts: Designed by Cass Gilbert and nicknamed the Cathedral of Commerce.
F. W. Woolworth reportedly paid for it in cash.
It was the world's tallest building until 1930. Its upper floors are now condos.

name: Grand Central Terminal
facts: The constellations on the Main Concourse ceiling are painted in reverse, as if seen from outside the sky.
Restorers left one small dark patch on the ceiling uncleaned to show how grimy it had become.
Two people whispering into opposite corners of the arches near the Oyster Bar can hear each other.

news.text: For two days in August, Vanderbilt Hall hosted “What Grows Here,” a free installation where visitors added their own stories to a living field of wheat.
Grand Central planned a 250-seat Osteria Centrale and Mercato Centrale in a former Rite Aid space, plus a grab-and-go counter carved from a 95-square-foot elevator shaft.

name: The Players
facts: The actor Edwin Booth founded this private club for actors and artists in 1888.
Booth was the brother of John Wilkes Booth, Lincoln's assassin.
Stanford White remodeled the house for the club.

news.text: In August, The Players promoted guided tours of its landmark clubhouse, featuring Edwin Booth’s conserved bedroom suite, the pool room where Mark Twain played, and 18th-century stage props and costumes.
The Players was set to open its clubhouse to the public for one night on September 24 for For the Record 2026, a battle of bands benefiting music education.

name: 34 Gramercy Park East
facts: Completed in 1883, it's one of the oldest cooperative apartment buildings still standing in New York.
Its residents are among those who can hold a key to Gramercy Park.

name: Gramercy Park
facts: Samuel Ruggles laid out the park in 1831 and sold the lots around it with park access attached.
It's still private. Only residents of the surrounding lots can get a key, and the locks are changed regularly.
It is one of only two private parks in New York City.
The gates traditionally open to the public for carolers on Christmas Eve, one of the few times outsiders can step inside.

news.text: On July 13, a judge sided with the Gramercy Park Hotel in its rooftop dispute with a neighboring co-op and lifted a halt on hotel construction.
By August 24, union crews were restoring the hotel’s interior, installing floor coverings, acoustical ceilings and interior systems across multiple floors.

name: The Ansonia
facts: Its developer, W. E. D. Stokes, kept a small farm on the roof with chickens, ducks and goats, and sold fresh eggs to tenants.
Babe Ruth lived here.

news.text: A September 25, 2026 report noted that *American Horror Story: 13* modeled its fictional Apollyon apartment building on The Ansonia’s facade.

name: 75½ Bedford Street
facts: Often called the narrowest house in New York, at about 9½ feet wide.
The poet Edna St. Vincent Millay lived here in the 1920s.
Edna St. Vincent Millay wrote “The Ballad of the Harp-Weaver” in Europe in 1922, not at 75½ Bedford Street; the house plaque wrongly says otherwise.
The house’s literary charm is its studio: a 1923 renovation added a skylight and turned the top floor into a studio for Millay.

name: Morris–Jumel Mansion
facts: Built in 1765, it's the oldest surviving house in Manhattan.
George Washington used it as his headquarters in the fall of 1776.
Visitors have long reported sightings of Eliza Jumel, its famous former owner.

name: St. Paul's Chapel
facts: The oldest surviving church building in Manhattan.
George Washington prayed here after his inauguration in 1789.
It survived September 11 with little damage and served as a relief center for recovery workers.

name: Fraunces Tavern
facts: George Washington said farewell to his officers here in December 1783.
The building you see today is largely a 1907 reconstruction.

name: The Plaza
facts: Opened in 1907, designed by Henry J. Hardenbergh.
Home of Eloise, the girl from Kay Thompson's children's books who lives on the top floor.

name: Hook & Ladder 8
facts: A working FDNY firehouse.
It played the Ghostbusters' headquarters in the 1984 film, and the crew displays a Ghostbusters sign inside.

name: 90 Bedford Street
facts: Its corner exterior appeared as the apartment building in Friends.

name: 66 Perry Street
facts: Its stoop stood in for Carrie Bradshaw's in Sex and the City.
Fans visit so often that the owners have put up a chain to keep them off the steps.

name: Tom's Restaurant
facts: The diner's exterior stood in for Monk's Café in Seinfeld.
It also inspired Suzanne Vega's song "Tom's Diner."

name: 169 East 71st Street
facts: Holly Golightly's brownstone in Breakfast at Tiffany's (1961).

name: 55 Central Park West
facts: Dana Barrett's building in Ghostbusters, where the film's rooftop showdown takes place.
For the movie, the top floors were extended with models and matte paintings.

name: Merchant's House Museum
facts: The Tredwell family lived here for almost a century, and the house survives with much of their furniture.
It's often called the most haunted house in Manhattan. Gertrude Tredwell, the last of the family, is said to linger.

name: Theodore Roosevelt Birthplace
facts: Theodore Roosevelt was born on this site in 1858.
The original house was demolished. This is a reconstruction built in 1923.

name: Cooper Union Foundation Building
facts: Abraham Lincoln gave his Cooper Union speech in the Great Hall in 1860.
Peter Cooper built in a round elevator shaft before passenger elevators were in common use.

name: Radio City Music Hall
facts: Opened in 1932 and home to the Rockettes.
When it opened, it was the largest indoor theater in the world.

name: Katz's Delicatessen
facts: Katz's traces its founding to 1888.
The famous diner scene in When Harry Met Sally (1989) was filmed here. A sign marks the table.
During World War II its slogan was "Send a salami to your boy in the army," and it still ships salamis today.

name: Trinity Church
facts: Alexander Hamilton is buried in the churchyard.
When it was finished in 1846, its spire was the tallest point in New York City.

name: Federal Hall
facts: George Washington took the oath as the first U.S. president on this site in 1789.
The earlier building where he was sworn in was demolished. Today's temple-front building opened in 1842 as the Custom House.

name: New York Stock Exchange
facts: The Broad Street building opened in 1903, with a sculpted pediment called Integrity Protecting the Works of Man.
Traders first met under a buttonwood tree on Wall Street in 1792.

name: Alexander Hamilton U.S. Custom House
facts: Designed by Cass Gilbert, who later designed the Woolworth Building.
The four statues out front, by Daniel Chester French, represent four continents.
It now houses a Smithsonian museum of Native American history and culture.

name: 40 Wall Street
facts: In 1930 it briefly claimed the title of world's tallest building.
It lost within weeks, when the Chrysler Building raised its secretly built spire.

name: Federal Reserve Bank of New York
facts: Its gold vault sits about 80 feet below street level, on Manhattan's bedrock.
It holds one of the largest stores of gold in the world, most of it owned by foreign governments.

name: City Hall
facts: Completed in 1812, it's the oldest city hall in the United States that still houses its original government functions.
Abraham Lincoln's body lay in state in the rotunda in 1865.

name: Manhattan Municipal Building
facts: A gilded statue called Civic Fame stands on top.
A subway station is built right into its base.

name: Haughwout Building
facts: In 1857 it got the world's first commercial passenger elevator, built by Elisha Otis.
Its cast-iron facade was designed to imitate a Venetian palace.

name: Old St. Patrick's Cathedral
facts: It was New York's Catholic cathedral until the Fifth Avenue cathedral opened in 1879.
There are catacombs beneath the church.
The baptism scene in The Godfather was filmed here.

name: Nom Wah Tea Parlor
facts: Serving dim sum on Doyers Street since 1920, it's one of Chinatown's oldest restaurants.
Doyers Street's sharp bend was once nicknamed the Bloody Angle.

name: Edward Mooney House
facts: Built around 1785 to 1789, it's the oldest surviving townhouse in Manhattan.
It went up just after the British left New York at the end of the Revolution.

name: Tenement Museum
facts: About 7,000 people from some 20 countries lived at 97 Orchard Street between 1863 and 1935.
The upper floors were sealed up for decades, which preserved them for the museum.

name: Eldridge Street Synagogue
facts: One of the first great synagogues built in America by Jewish immigrants from Eastern Europe.
After a 20-year restoration, a new stained-glass window by Kiki Smith was installed in 2010.

name: Russ & Daughters
facts: A family-run appetizing shop, selling smoked fish and bagels on Houston Street for about a century.
It was one of the first businesses in America to put "& Daughters" in its name.

name: McSorley's Old Ale House
facts: It claims to date to 1854, which would make it one of the city's oldest bars.
Women weren't allowed in until a 1970 court ruling.
It serves just two kinds of beer: light and dark.
Dusty wishbones hang over the bar. Legend says soldiers hung them before leaving for World War I, and the ones left belonged to men who never came back.

name: St. Mark's Church in-the-Bowery
facts: Peter Stuyvesant, the last Dutch governor of New Amsterdam, is buried in a vault here.
It stands on land that was once his farm, or bouwerij, which gave the Bowery its name.

name: CBGB
facts: The club at 315 Bowery helped launch punk and new wave: the Ramones, Talking Heads, Blondie and Patti Smith all played here.
CBGB stood for Country, BlueGrass and Blues, the music its owner originally planned to book.

name: Physical Graffiti buildings
facts: 96 and 98 St. Marks Place appear on the cover of Led Zeppelin's 1975 album Physical Graffiti.
The buildings actually have five stories. One was cropped out so they'd fit the square album cover.

name: Stonewall Inn
facts: The 1969 Stonewall uprising here is widely seen as the start of the modern LGBTQ rights movement.
In 2016 it became the first U.S. national monument dedicated to LGBTQ history.

name: Jefferson Market Library
facts: It opened in 1877 as a courthouse.
Its clock tower once served as a fire lookout.
Neighbors saved it from demolition, and it reopened as a public library in 1967.

name: Chumley's
facts: A Prohibition-era speakeasy with an unmarked entrance.
Legend says the bar term "86" (to throw someone out) comes from its 86 Bedford Street address, where patrons slipped out when police arrived. Etymologists doubt it.

name: Cherry Lane Theatre
facts: Converted into a theater in 1924, it's one of New York's oldest continuously running off-Broadway theaters.
The building started out as a brewery and later a box factory.

name: Isaacs-Hendricks House
facts: Built in 1799, it's the oldest house in Greenwich Village.
It's the next-door neighbor of 75½ Bedford Street, often called the city's narrowest house.

name: White Horse Tavern
facts: Dylan Thomas drank here shortly before he fell ill at the Hotel Chelsea in 1953.
It was a favorite of writers including Jack Kerouac and James Baldwin.

name: Electric Lady Studios
facts: Jimi Hendrix built this recording studio and opened it in 1970, weeks before his death.
Artists from Stevie Wonder to Daft Punk have recorded here.

name: Chelsea Market
facts: This was the National Biscuit Company (Nabisco) factory.
The Oreo cookie was invented here in 1912.

name: Met Life Tower
facts: From 1909 to 1913 it was the tallest building in the world.
It was modeled on the Campanile in Venice's St. Mark's Square.

name: Tammany Hall
facts: Built as headquarters for Tammany Hall, the Democratic political machine that dominated city politics for decades.
The machine's name came from Tamanend, a Lenape leader.

name: National Arts Club
facts: This was the home of Samuel Tilden, governor of New York and 1876 presidential candidate.
He reportedly feared for his safety and added steel doors, and a tunnel to 19th Street is part of the house's lore.

name: Pete's Tavern
facts: It claims to be one of the city's oldest continuously operating bars, stretching back to 1864.
Legend says O. Henry wrote The Gift of the Magi in one of its booths.

name: New York Public Library
facts: The marble lions out front are named Patience and Fortitude. Mayor Fiorello La Guardia gave them those names in the 1930s.
It opened in 1911 on the site of the old Croton reservoir.

name: St. Patrick's Cathedral
facts: Dedicated in 1879, when this part of Fifth Avenue was still on the edge of town.
It replaced Old St. Patrick's on Mulberry Street as the city's Catholic cathedral.

name: Algonquin Hotel
facts: Dorothy Parker and friends met for lunch here in the 1920s as the Algonquin Round Table.
The hotel has kept a resident cat for decades. The males are named Hamlet and the females Matilda.
E. B. White wrote his 1948 essay Here Is New York while staying at the hotel.

name: 30 Rockefeller Plaza
facts: The famous 1932 photo Lunch atop a Skyscraper shows ironworkers on a beam during its construction.
NBC's studios here are home to Saturday Night Live.
Construction workers put up the first Christmas tree here in 1931. The official tree lighting began in 1933.

name: Carnegie Hall
facts: Tchaikovsky conducted on opening night in 1891.
It was nearly torn down in 1960 before a campaign led by violinist Isaac Stern saved it.

name: New Amsterdam Theatre
facts: Home of the Ziegfeld Follies for years.
Staff tell stories of Olive Thomas, a Follies star, whose ghost is said to walk the theater.

name: Macy's Herald Square
facts: Setting of the film Miracle on 34th Street (1947).
The store's wooden escalators, some of the first of their kind, are still running.
The Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade, first held in 1924, ends in front of the store.

name: United Nations Headquarters
facts: The land is under UN control by agreement with the United States.
The UN issues its own postage stamps, valid only when mailed from the building.

name: Seagram Building
facts: Designed by Ludwig Mies van der Rohe.
It was set back from Park Avenue behind a plaza, a choice that helped shape the city's 1961 zoning rules.

name: The Morgan Library
facts: Built for financier J. P. Morgan's private library.
During the Panic of 1907, Morgan locked bankers in the library overnight until they agreed to a rescue plan.

name: Ed Sullivan Theater
facts: The Beatles made their American TV debut here on The Ed Sullivan Show in February 1964.
It later became home to The Late Show, first with David Letterman and then Stephen Colbert.

name: Sardi's
facts: Its walls are covered in hundreds of caricatures of Broadway stars.
Opening-night casts have traditionally waited here for the reviews.

name: Hearst Tower
facts: The six-story base from 1928 was meant to support a tower that wasn't built for almost 80 years.
Norman Foster's diagonal-grid tower was finished on top of it in 2006.

name: Tiffany & Co. Fifth Avenue
facts: Audrey Hepburn eats a pastry at its windows in the opening scene of Breakfast at Tiffany's (1961).
A statue of Atlas holding a clock sits over the entrance. It moved here from an earlier Tiffany store.

name: The San Remo
facts: Its twin towers, designed by Emery Roth, are a signature of the Central Park West skyline.
Its co-op board has famously turned down celebrity buyers.

name: American Museum of Natural History
facts: Founded in 1869. Theodore Roosevelt's father was one of its founders.
The Night at the Museum films are set here.

name: The Apthorp
facts: A full-block apartment building built around a private central courtyard with fountains.
Its courtyard has appeared in many films.

name: Riverside Church
facts: Its tower makes it the tallest church in the United States.
The tower holds a carillon of 74 bells, including one of the largest tuned bells in the world.

name: Cathedral of St. John the Divine
facts: Construction began in 1892 and still isn't finished, which earned it the nickname St. John the Unfinished.
Peacocks roam the grounds.

name: Café Lalo
facts: Tom Hanks waits for Meg Ryan here in You've Got Mail (1998).

name: Guggenheim Museum
facts: Frank Lloyd Wright's only major building in New York City.
Wright worked on the design for about 15 years and died six months before it opened.

name: Gracie Mansion
facts: Built as a country house in 1799, when this was far outside the city.
It has been the mayor's official residence since Fiorello La Guardia moved in, in 1942.

name: The Frick
facts: Built as the home of industrialist Henry Clay Frick, who planned from the start for it to become a museum.
It opened to the public in 1935.

name: Carnegie Mansion
facts: Andrew Carnegie's home, now the Cooper Hewitt design museum.
It was one of the first private homes in the U.S. with a structural steel frame and a residential Otis elevator.

name: Mount Vernon Hotel Museum
facts: Built in 1799 as a carriage house.
From 1826 to 1833 it was a day hotel where city dwellers escaped to the countryside, which was then this part of Manhattan.

name: Apollo Theater
facts: Its Amateur Night has run since the 1930s and launched Ella Fitzgerald.
Performers rub a stump from the Tree of Hope, which once stood nearby, for luck before they go on.

name: Hotel Theresa
facts: Called the Waldorf of Harlem.
Fidel Castro stayed here during his 1960 visit to the United Nations, and Nikita Khrushchev came to meet him.
It stopped operating as a hotel in the 1960s and was converted to offices.

name: Hamilton Grange
facts: Alexander Hamilton's country home, the only house he ever owned.
It has been moved twice, most recently in 2008, when it was lifted and rolled into St. Nicholas Park.

name: Minton's Playhouse
facts: Late-night jam sessions here in the 1940s with Thelonious Monk, Dizzy Gillespie and Charlie Parker helped create bebop.

name: Langston Hughes House
facts: The poet Langston Hughes lived and worked on the top floor for the last 20 years of his life.
Langston Hughes wrote *Montage of a Dream Deferred* (1951) from his private study on the house’s third floor.
Langston Hughes lived and worked on the rowhouse’s top floor from 1947 to 1967; works he wrote there include *Montage of a Dream Deferred* (1951) and *I Wonder as I Wander* (1956).
A charming detail: Hughes once said, “I would rather have a kitchenette in Harlem than a mansion in Westchester.”

name: United Palace
facts: One of Loew's five Wonder Theatres, the lavish movie palaces the chain built around New York.
Its interior mixes Moorish, Indian and other styles in one room.

name: The Cloisters
facts: Parts of several medieval European monasteries were shipped over and rebuilt here.
John D. Rockefeller Jr. also bought the Palisades across the river so the view would stay unspoiled.

name: The Octagon
facts: The domed rotunda was the entrance to the New York City Lunatic Asylum on what was then Blackwell's Island.
Journalist Nellie Bly went undercover in the asylum in 1887 and exposed its conditions.

name: Castle Williams
facts: A round sandstone fort on Governors Island, finished in 1811 to guard the harbor.
It later served as a military prison.

name: Statue of Liberty
facts: Liberty Island is part of the borough of Manhattan.
Gustave Eiffel designed the iron framework inside.

name: Ellis Island
facts: About 12 million immigrants passed through between 1892 and 1954.
The main building opened in 1900, after a fire destroyed the first one.

name: Hessian Military Hut
facts: In 1915, amateur archaeologist Reginald Pelham Bolton dismantled a hut from the Revolutionary War encampment and rebuilt its foundation here.
Prince Frederick II sold Hessian soldiers’ services to Britain without their consent; Northern Manhattan’s huts held up to eight men each.
Bolton excavated a Revolutionary-era encampment of more than 60 huts; developers demolished the others to make way for apartment houses.

name: James Watson House
facts: The 1806 addition follows State Street’s curve, and its upper Ionic columns were believed to have been made from ships’ masts.
In 1885, Rev. John J. Riordan bought Watson House for a mission protecting Irish immigrant girls. The Archdiocese says the mission helped more than 100,000 women.
James Watson built the house in 1793. Elizabeth Ann Seton lived next door at No. 8, where she bore her fifth and last child.

name: 27 Harrison Street House
facts: John McComb designed and built the house as his own residence, completing it in 1797; he also designed City Hall and Alexander Hamilton’s country house, The Grange.
The house originally stood at 317 Washington Street, in a cove on the south side of a small point only 100 feet from the river.
When the neighborhood became an urban-renewal area, the Landmarks Commission chose to save the houses; they were moved to Harrison Street and offered with unfinished interiors in 1975.

name: Mount Vernon Hotel Museum & Garden
facts: Col. William Stephens Smith, a former George Washington aide, named the estate for Washington’s Virginia home; financial difficulties led people to dub it “Smith’s Folly.”
It was one of about 50 day hotels around New York, where visitors escaped downtown for music, dancing, games, carriage rides and hearty meals; today it is the only historic site interpreting them.
A New York Tribune article in the museum’s archives reported an unidentified skeleton under the 1799 carriage house’s floorboards, leaving its identity a mystery.

name: 94 Greenwich Street House
facts: Owner Augustine Hicks Lawrence signed the 1792 Buttonwood Agreement, one of 24 men who established the New York Stock and Exchange Board, predecessor to the New York Stock Exchange.
By 1850, directories listed the Union Hotel here alongside a porterhouse; the proprietor, his wife, daughter, and twelve other residents lived in the building.
The house gained a full story before 1858, yet its original gambrel roof outline remains visible on the Rector Street facade.

name: Jonas Wood House
facts: Jonas Wood bought the lot from Trinity in 1795 for $395, and an 1804 city directory listed him at the address, indicating construction in 1803, 04.
A preservation project moved the former 314 Washington Street house to Harrison Street in 1975; critic Paul Goldberger later mocked the recreated facades, saying Disneyland’s looked more real.
The LPC found that the house retains its original roof, dormers, and cornice, with nearly all surviving early-19th-century detail above the altered first floor.

name: Stuyvesant-Fish House
facts: Nicholas Fish hosted General Lafayette at the house on September 10, 1824, during Lafayette’s celebrated return to America, fifty years after the Revolutionary War.
Hamilton Fish was born in the house in 1808 and later served as New York governor, U.S. senator, and secretary of state for eight years.
At 18, Nicholas Fish became a major, and the designation report identifies him as possibly the youngest major in U.S. Army history; he also served as an executor of Alexander Hamilton’s estate.

name: 2 White Street House
facts: Gideon Tucker built the house in 1809 in an old-fashioned Dutch style, even as Federal-style homes rose elsewhere; its original gambrel roof and dormers survive.
Rev. Theodore S. Wright, a prominent Black abolitionist minister, lived here from 1842 until his death in 1847; the house may have served as a stop on the Underground Railroad.
Around the Civil War, the basement reportedly housed a dance hall called “Shadow City,” a surprising chapter in the little house’s changing uses.

name: Former St. George’s Syrian Catholic Church
facts: A 1859 newspaper described 103 Washington Street as a German dance-house. Sailor-oriented dance halls sometimes doubled as places where women arranged sex work while waltzing.
The former church is Little Syria’s most significant surviving remnant, recalling Washington Street’s role as the “Mother Colony” for Syrian immigrant communities across America.
Lebanese-American draftsman Harvey F. Cassab designed the church’s 1929, 30 Neo-Gothic façade in bright white terra cotta. Its colorful relief shows St. George slaying a green dragon.

name: 57 Sullivan Street House
facts: Frederick Youmans, a carter, built the house as a speculative venture between 1816 and 1817; his business supplied fill for public projects, and the Landmarks Commission identifies no architect.

The Knickerbocker, a basement bar run by African-American bartender Charles Woodbeck, served a multiracial clientele. In 1875, four customers were arrested for robbery and assault; one, Isaac Hatch, had been acquitted of murdering a policeman.
A 1827 sale ad called the two-story house “nearly new” and listed a brick cistern, a yard in good order, and a billiard table, a charming glimpse of its early domestic life.

name: Stephen Van Rensselaer House
facts: The house stood at 153 Mulberry Street from its 1816 completion for Stephen Van Rensselaer until it shifted to No. 149 in 1841.
When the city landmarked it in 1969, the house had one of Manhattan’s few remaining gambrel roofs.
Its stoop preserves some original wrought-iron handrails, while cast-iron panels above the top step show wreaths, bows, and arrows.

name: James Brown House
facts: During Prohibition, John Rolandi ran a restaurant at the front and a secret speakeasy at the back; upstairs rooms were frequently used as a brothel.
Owners circumvented landmark façade rules by painting the edge of the neon “BAR” sign so it read “EAR,” also referencing the music journal Rip Hayman once ran upstairs.
Local legend gives the Ear Inn a sailor ghost named Mickey; some versions say a car struck him outside, while others claim he died at his barstool.

name: 27A Harrison Street House
facts: John McComb built 27A Harrison Street, then 315 Washington Street, in 1819. He was New York City’s first native-born architect and designed City Hall and Alexander Hamilton’s country house, The Grange.
The lot occupies part of a 62-acre farm granted in 1636 to Annetje Jans and her first husband, both Scandinavian-born; Queen Anne gave the farm to Trinity Church in 1705.

The house stood at 315 Washington Street until urban-renewal plans threatened its block; preservationists moved it to Harrison Street with two other Washington Street houses, then rebuilt their exteriors in 1975.

name: Church of the Holy Communion
facts: Consecrated in 1846 as an Episcopal church, designed by Richard Upjohn, who also designed Trinity Church.
In the 1980s it became the Limelight, one of the city's most famous nightclubs.
It has since been converted to shops and a gym.

name: Puck Building
facts: Built in 1886 to print Puck, a popular humor magazine.
A gilded statue of the character Puck still stands over the entrance.
The old printing plant now holds offices, shops and penthouse homes added on the roof.

name: Engine Company 31
facts: Built in 1895 as a firehouse, designed to look like a French Renaissance chateau.
After the fire company moved out in the 1970s, it became home to the Downtown Community Television Center.

name: Scribner Building
facts: Built in 1913 as the headquarters and bookstore of Charles Scribner's Sons, the publisher of Hemingway and F. Scott Fitzgerald.
The bookstore closed in 1989. Its landmarked glass-and-iron storefront now holds other shops.

name: 454 West 20th Street
facts: In April 1951 Jack Kerouac typed the first full draft of On the Road here, on one long roll of paper, in about three weeks.
Jack Kerouac completed On the Road in April 1951 while living at 454 West 20th Street.
Kerouac wrote it on a long roll of teletype paper.

name: 337 Bleecker Street
facts: Lorraine Hansberry wrote A Raisin in the Sun while living here in the 1950s.

name: 53rd & 3rd
facts: The Ramones named their 1976 song "53rd & 3rd" for this intersection.

name: Queensboro Bridge
facts: It opened in 1909 and is also known as the 59th Street Bridge.
Simon & Garfunkel named "The 59th Street Bridge Song (Feelin' Groovy)" for it in 1966.

name: 82 Washington Place
facts: Richard Wright wrote his autobiography, Black Boy, here in 1945.
The building’s tenants swap its windowsill plants for holiday wreaths.

name: Pete’s Tavern
facts: Poets & Writers says O. Henry (William Sydney Porter) supposedly wrote “The Gift of the Magi” in Pete’s booth in 1905, while the tavern still bore the name Healy’s.
Tavern lore places the writing in a booth adorned with photographs and a handwritten letter; the Smithsonian says no official documentation confirms O. Henry wrote it there.

name: Allen Ginsberg & Peter Orlovsky Residence
facts: Allen Ginsberg wrote most of “Kaddish” there in 1959, in memory of his mother.
A January 1960 photograph shows Ginsberg at his apartment typewriter; another shows him with his Siamese cat.

name: Emma Lazarus's former home
facts: Emma Lazarus wrote “The New Colossus” at her home at 18 West 10th Street on November 2, 1883.

Writer Constance Cory Harrison asked Lazarus to contribute verses to an exhibition and auction that would raise funds to complete the Statue of Liberty’s pedestal. Lazarus wrote the resulting sonnet from home.

name: 240 Central Park South Apartments
facts: Britannica identifies Antoine de Saint-Exupéry as the writer of The Little Prince and says it appeared in English and French in April 1943.
The New York State Literary Tree places Saint-Exupéry at 240 Central Park South while he wrote The Little Prince.
Saint-Exupéry often wrote late at night with a cigarette and coffee or tea, and called friends at 2 a.m. to read pages aloud.
